opus-5.5.text:
Well, I have enormous respect for Chomsky. He's one of the towering intellectual figures of the twentieth century, and the Chomsky hierarchy is a genuinely beautiful piece of work. It gave us a precise way to think about what different classes of machines can and can't compute. That's lasting.

But I think his broader program for language, and by extension his view of what AI can or can't tell us, has been substantially undercut by what we've seen over the past several years.

The core of the Chomskyan view is that language is fundamentally about syntax, about an innate, specialized faculty, a universal grammar, that's wired in because the input children get is supposedly too impoverished to learn from. That's the poverty of the stimulus argument. Statistical learning, on this view, is a dead end. You can't get to real linguistic competence just by soaking up patterns.

Then large language models came along and did essentially the thing that was supposed to be impossible. They learned grammar, and a great deal more than grammar, from exposure alone, with no built-in universal grammar. Now, you can quibble. They see far more text than a child hears, and that's a fair point. But the in-principle claim, that this kind of learning simply can't get you there, looks very hard to sustain.

Chomsky's response has been to say these models are just "plagiarism engines," or that they tell us nothing about language because they could equally learn impossible languages. I find that unpersuasive. Partly because it's an empirical claim that's turned out to be shakier than asserted, and partly because it sets the bar somewhere no system, including a human brain, could clear. Brains are also statistical learners embedded in a body and a social world.

I think the deeper issue is that he separated competence from performance and syntax from meaning, and treated the formal skeleton as the real thing and everything else as noise. My own view is almost the reverse. Language is a social, predictive, deeply contextual phenomenon. Meaning comes from use, from modeling other minds, from prediction. Syntax is part of that, but it's not the hidden essence beneath it.

So I'd say Chomsky asked the right questions and gave us beautiful formal tools, but on the central question of how language is learned and what intelligence is made of, I think the evidence has gone the other way. And to his credit, he made claims that were clear enough to be tested. That's more than many theorists do.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I have a complicated relationship with Chomsky's work, and I think a lot of people in the field do. Let me start by saying he's enormously important. The idea that language has a formal structure you can study mathematically, the Chomsky hierarchy, the whole program of taking syntax seriously as a computational object rather than just a set of social conventions, that was a real revolution. It gave us a lot of the vocabulary we still use. And the critique of behaviorism was right. Skinner really was wrong that you could get language out of pure stimulus-response conditioning.

But I think the program went wrong in a couple of ways that have become very obvious now that we actually have machines that use language fluently.

The first is the insistence on an innate universal grammar, this idea that there's a dedicated language organ with a very specific, very rich set of syntactic rules wired in by evolution, and that the input a child gets is too impoverished to learn language from. The "poverty of the stimulus" argument. I never found that convincing, and large language models are, to me, pretty close to a decisive empirical refutation. These systems are trained on text alone, with no built-in grammar, no parse trees, no notion of a noun phrase, and they end up producing and understanding grammatical language across every human language we throw at them. Now, yes, they see far more text than a child does, and the learning algorithm is different. But the claim wasn't just that children are efficient learners. The claim was that grammar is in principle unlearnable from data. That's just not true. A general-purpose statistical learner can get there.

The second problem is the sharp separation between syntax and everything else, between competence and performance, between the formal system and meaning. Chomsky treated language as this abstract generative device, and treated the messy, probabilistic, context-dependent stuff as noise to be factored out. "Colorless green ideas sleep furiously" was supposed to show that grammaticality is independent of probability and meaning. But what we've learned is that prediction, statistics, and meaning are all entangled. If you want to predict the next word well, you have to model what the speaker is talking about, what they believe, what the world is like. Syntax falls out of that. It's not the foundation, it's an emergent regularity.

And this connects to his dismissal of the whole statistical and connectionist tradition. There's that famous line about how a statistical approach to language is like using statistics to predict the weather instead of understanding the physics. He's been very dismissive of machine learning, saying these models tell us nothing about language or cognition because they'd learn impossible languages just as readily as possible ones. I think that's partly an empirical question, and the early evidence suggests they actually don't learn impossible languages as easily. But more fundamentally, I think he has a view of what counts as "understanding" that's very theory-first. If you can't write down the rule, it doesn't count. And I think that's backwards. Brains don't work by writing down rules either.

I'd put it this way. Chomsky was asking the right question, which is how can a finite system produce and comprehend an unbounded range of sentences. His answer was recursion plus innate structure. The answer that's actually turned out to work is massively parallel prediction over sequences, learned from experience, where the structure is distributed across billions of parameters rather than stated as rules. Those are both computational theories of language. His is just the one that didn't pan out.

What I find a bit frustrating is that rather than engaging with that, the response from Chomsky and his circle has largely been to redefine the goalposts. These systems are "just" stochastic parrots, they're "just" doing autocomplete, they don't really understand. I think that's a mistake. If something generates and interprets language at human level, and you want to say it's not doing language, you owe an account of what language is that excludes it, and I haven't seen one that doesn't also exclude a lot of what humans do.

So, enormous respect for the foundational contribution. But I think his specific model of how language works, and his broader stance on what computation can tell us about the mind, have aged badly. And honestly, I think a scientist of his stature should be more excited than he is. We finally have a working artifact to study. That should be thrilling.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to separate Chomsky’s contribution from the question of whether his approach gives us the right account of intelligence. Formal grammars were an enormously productive way to think about language. But specifying which sentences a grammar can generate is different from explaining how a person learns to speak, understands someone else, or uses language in the world.

The disagreement becomes especially interesting around learning. How much structure has to be supplied in advance, and how much can emerge from experience? Language models give us a reason to revisit strong claims about what learning can’t accomplish. They acquire a remarkable amount of linguistic structure without being explicitly given the grammatical rules that a Chomskyan account might lead us to emphasize.

That doesn’t establish that children learn the same way. Children have bodies, social relationships, and very different experiences from a model trained on text. Nor does fluent output settle every question about understanding. But I think the productive response is to investigate what these systems have learned, where they generalize, and where they fail. A theory of language should be answerable to those observations, rather than treating their possibility as something we can decide in advance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Chomsky made an enormously important contribution by treating language as something you could study formally and computationally. But I would separate that contribution from the claim that a particular formal account of grammar explains how language works in the brain.

A grammar can describe which sentences belong to a language without explaining how a child learns it, how meaning arises, or how we use language together. Those are different questions. And if you build your theory around an idealized speaker, you risk setting aside precisely the variation and interaction that a learning system needs to explain.

The interesting thing about modern language models is that they put pressure on some strong claims about what can be learned from linguistic experience. They don’t settle every question about human cognition, and predicting text is not a complete theory of language. But their capabilities are evidence that we should take seriously. If a system learns something that your theory says it couldn’t learn that way, that’s an opportunity to reconsider the theory.
